comment: Offline smoke corpus: book-ish prose passages plus two query workloads. kind=paraphrase queries share almost no vocabulary with their gold doc (the documented ese weak spot, docs/spikes/chat-spike.md); kind=known-item queries are the short remembered-phrase lookups a personal library actually gets, using words present in the gold doc. Each query names exactly one gold doc.

docs.text: Simmer the stock uncovered over a low flame, letting the liquid diminish by half. As the water departs, what remains gains body and clings to the back of a spoon, ready to nap the roast.
Set the shaped loaf in a warm corner of the kitchen, draped with a damp cloth. The dough is ready for the oven when a gentle press of the finger springs back slowly, leaving only a faint dimple.
Draw the blade across the stone at a shallow, constant angle, alternating sides with even strokes. A burr forming along the edge tells you the two bevels have finally met.
Whisk the yolks while adding the oil a drop at a time; hurry and the mixture will split into a greasy puddle. Patience binds the two into a thick, glossy cream.

After cooking, wipe the pan with coarse salt and a dry rag rather than soap. Rub in a thin film of fat and warm it on the stove until it smokes faintly, and the black surface will only improve with the years.

The escapement releases the wheel train one tooth at a time, each release nudging the balance to keep it swinging. It is the heartbeat of the watch, converting stored force into a steady count of moments.
Turning the crown coils a ribbon of steel ever tighter inside its barrel. This stored tension, doled out through the gears, is the only sustenance the movement receives between windings.

A rod of brass lengthens in summer heat, and a longer pendulum swings more slowly, so the clock falls behind in July. Makers answered with gridiron rods of mixed metals whose expansions cancel one another.
Pivots of hardened steel turn in holes drilled through rubies, for the stone wears less than any metal and holds a film of oil in place. Thus a watch may run for decades before its bearings are cut.

The slender spiral above the balance must breathe evenly whether wound tight or nearly spent. Overcoiling its outer terminal brings the spring's center of gravity home and steadies the rate through the day.
The dhows leave the coast when the winds reverse in November, running before the northeast breeze to Zanzibar. Half the year the ocean pushes ships south, the other half it carries them home again.

The caravan moved by night, steering on stars the guides had known since childhood, and rested through the furnace of the afternoon. Wells three days apart dictated the route more surely than any map.

Above the high passes the porters chewed coca leaves and walked slowly, for hurry brings on the pounding head and sick stomach that the mountains inflict on those who climb too fast. The only cure is to descend.

Where the rapids turned to white spray between the rocks, we unloaded the canoes and carried boats and baggage along the forest trail, returning twice for the remaining bundles before the river grew calm enough to float again.

The harbor empties twice a day, leaving vessels sitting upright in the mud until the flood returns. A captain who misreads the tables will find his keel gripped fast for six hours within sight of open water.
The swifts arrive with the warm weather and are gone by August, having crossed two continents in the interval. A bird ringed in an English belfry was recovered the same winter south of the Congo.
The round growths on oak twigs are not fruit but nurseries: a tiny wasp pricks the bud and the tree, provoked, swells around the egg, feeding and housing the larva that consumes it from within.

By felling aspens across the stream the animals raise the water into a pond that drowns the entrances of their lodge, keeping wolves from the door. The dam is patched each autumn with mud and fresh branches.
What appears a single crust on the boulder is two organisms in partnership: a fungus giving shelter and a colony of algae paying rent in sugar made from sunlight. Neither thrives on the stone alone.
Between the tide marks the shore is ruled in bands: barnacles crowd the upper rocks that dry for hours, mussels hold the middle, and the anemones keep below, where the sea rarely leaves them.

As the visitor nears the sun its ices boil away, and the escaping dust is pushed always away from the sun by the pressure of light itself. Hence the tail does not trail behind but points sunward-opposite, even as the comet retreats.

Observe a nearby star in January and again in June, and it will seem to shift against the deeper background, for the earth has moved to the far side of its orbit. From that tiny displacement the star's distance is measured in trigonometry.

Though the moon keeps one face toward us, it rocks gently in its orbit, sometimes showing a sliver beyond the eastern limb, sometimes the western. Patient observers may map somewhat more than half the globe.
Layer the green cuttings with dry straw and a little soil, and turn the pile when it cools. In a season the garden's refuse becomes a dark, sweet-smelling crumble that feeds the beds it came from.

A twig cut from the prized apple is bound into a cleft on the rootstock, cambium touching cambium, and sealed with wax. If the union takes, the young tree will bear fruit identical to its parent, which seed can never promise.

Each letter is cast on its own small block of metal, assembled into lines, locked in a frame, inked, and pressed. When the run is finished the page is broken up and the same letters are marshalled into new words.
Sheets left unsized drink ink like a napkin, the strokes feathering into blots. A bath of gelatin closes the pores so the pen may glide and the letters keep their edges.

Lacking sight of land, the navigator keeps his position by arithmetic: so many hours on such a heading at such a speed, marked daily on the chart. Currents and leeway conspire to make a liar of him, so a landfall is always a small act of faith.
A ship long in warm waters gathers a garden on her bottom — weed and barnacles that drag at every mile. Captains careen their vessels on a convenient beach to scrape and pay the planks with tallow.

The bark of a Peruvian tree, ground and taken in wine, quiets the recurring fevers of the marsh country. The Jesuits carried the powder to Europe, where it became worth more than silver in the sickly ports.

The old Cremonese masters brushed their instruments with a varnish whose recipe died with them. More than protection, the coat seems married to the tone, and chemists have chased its formula for two centuries.

Behind the gilded pipes a boy trod the bellows, keeping the wind chest full, for the grandest chord dies the instant the pressure fails. The music rested on his patient labor as surely as on the organist's hands.

The mold is buried in the casting pit and the bronze poured in one continuous stream, for a pause leaves a seam that will crack under the clapper. A great bell cools for a week before it may be struck.

A goblet taken hot from the blowpipe and left in the open air will shatter of its own accord, riven by inner strains. It must cool by slow degrees in the annealing oven, sometimes for days, before it can be trusted.

Packed in coarse salt, the herring will keep through the winter, for the brine draws the moisture that rot requires. The fish must be gutted the day of the catch or no quantity of salt will save them.
Blocks sawn from the frozen pond in January, stacked in the stone cellar and blanketed in sawdust, will last into August. The summer kitchen depends on winter's harvest.
The wicks are dipped in the melted tallow, lifted to harden, and dipped again, growing by thin coats until thick enough to burn the evening through. A hundred dippings make a decent candle.

The diggers followed the willow wand's dip and sank their shaft where it pointed, walling the sides with dry stone as they went. At thirty feet the sand grew dark, and by morning three feet of sweet water stood in the bottom.

Bundles of wheat straw are laid butt-down from the eaves upward, each course pinned with hazel spars, until the roof sheds rain like a bird's back. A well-laid coat will outlast the thatcher who combed it.

The boat glides into the stone chamber, the gates close behind, and water admitted from above lifts vessel and cargo together to the higher pound. By such watery staircases a barge climbs over the hills.

From hilltop towers the jointed arms spelled their message to the next station's telescope, and so on down the line. News that once rode three days on horseback reached Paris between breakfast and noon.

The miners carried caged canaries into the deep galleries, for the little birds faint at a whiff of the choking gas long before a man feels it. A silent cage was the signal to drop tools and run for the shaft.

The Frenchman's lens of stepped prisms gathers the lamp's scattered light and hurls it seaward in a single level beam, visible twenty miles off. A flame that once warned only the near shoals now serves the whole horizon.

Flour and water left on the sill soon begin to bubble with the wild leaven that lives on every grain. Fed daily, the pot of batter will raise bread for a lifetime, and bakers will their cultures to their children.

The wheels ripen in the cool of the limestone caverns, where the blue mold threads inward along the needle holes. The same milk aged in a dry loft makes a different cheese entirely; the cave is an ingredient.

The new-caught hawk is carried on the fist through crowded places, hooded and unhooded, fed only from the glove, until she takes the bustle of men calmly. This slow accustoming, and not hunger alone, makes her fit to fly free and return.

The black turf is sliced from the bog in brick-shaped sods and stood in little stacks to dry through the summer winds. Come winter it burns slow and smoky on the hearth, the stored sunlight of drowned forests.

The cocoons are drowned in the basin of hot water to loosen the gum, and the filaments of half a dozen are gathered and wound together onto the reel as a single thread. A mile of it may come from one worm's spinning.

No mortar holds the field walls, only the mason's eye for how each stone leans on its neighbors, through-stones tying the two faces into one. Built well, the wall breathes with the frost and stands two hundred years.
The bees work the purple thistle bloom through the driest weeks of summer, when every other flower has given up. The honey they make from it is pale, slow to candy, and tastes faintly of almonds.
